chief_complaint: severe vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration/ketones
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with severe vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration/ketones. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she has a prolonged stomach virus on top of regular morning sickness.
concerns: She is worried that her extreme dehydration will harm the baby and that missing work shifts will cause her to lose her retail job.
expectations: She hopes to get IV hydration, a prescription anti-vomiting medication, and a sick note for her employer.
social_hx: Does not use tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drugs during pregnancy

investigation_events.title: Urgent electrolyte assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: Urgent electrolyte results are now available. IV fluids with thiamine should not be delayed.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hyperemesis gravidarum is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Hyperemesis Gravidarum: IV fluids, thiamine, Pyridoxine/Doxylamine, Metoclopramide, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration/ketones

Key HPI features: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with severe vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration/ketones. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Hyperemesis Gravidarum.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hyperemesis gravidarum.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Normal nausea/vomiting of pregnancy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Dehydration.
management_principles: Plan for Hyperemesis Gravidarum: IV fluids, thiamine, Pyridoxine/Doxylamine, Metoclopramide
Arrange urgent obstetric assessment and consider hospital treatment for dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, or inability to tolerate oral intake
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of severe vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration/ketones. HPI: hyperemesis gravidarum.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Hyperemesis Gravidarum.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Hyperemesis Gravidarum.
reference_soap.plan: Assess vital signs, weight loss, urine ketones, and electrolytes. Give IV fluids with thiamine and use pregnancy-compatible antiemetics as clinically indicated. Arrange urgent obstetric assessment and consider hospital treatment for dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, or inability to tolerate oral intake.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Hyperemesis Gravidarum
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Hyperemesis Gravidarum
Implement evidence-based management plan: IV fluids, thiamine, Pyridoxine/Doxylamine, Metoclopramide

teaching.one_liner: Pregnant patient with severe vomiting, dehydration, ketonuria, and associated fatigue.

must_ask.say: How many weeks pregnant are you, and when did the vomiting start?
How many times a day are you vomiting, and can you keep fluids down?

must_ask.objective: Screen for dehydration and weight loss
must_ask.say: Have you lost weight, or felt dizzy and weak?
How is the fatigue affecting your daily activities?

must_ask.objective: Explain IV fluids and antiemetic treatment
must_ask.say: We'll give you IV fluids, thiamine, and medication to control the nausea.

history.answer: I am about eight weeks pregnant, and I have been vomiting constantly and cannot keep any food or water down. I feel completely drained, dizzy, and weak.
It started about two weeks ago as mild morning nausea, but over the past five days it has become relentless and happens all day long.
I am eight weeks pregnant with my first pregnancy, confirmed two weeks ago on an ultrasound.
I am vomiting more than eight to ten times a day, even when I have nothing left in my stomach.
Almost immediately after swallowing anything, even a sip of water, it comes right back up within five minutes.
It is mostly clear foamy fluid, yellowish-green bile, or the water I just drank. There is no blood, coffee grounds, or foul odor.
It happens continuously from morning until late at night, and it is not projectile vomiting that shoots across the room.
My abdominal muscles ache from retching so much, but I do not have any localized or cramping belly pain.
I have not had a bowel movement in three days because I cannot eat, but I am still passing gas and my belly is not bloated.
No, I have not had any diarrhea at all.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweating.
Nobody around me is sick, and my husband ate the exact same meals as me and feels perfectly fine.
No headache, no neck stiffness, and no confusion, but I feel very dizzy and unsteady when I stand up.
My vision is normal with no blurring, double vision, or flashing lights.
No, I have not bumped my head or had any falls or head injuries.
I cannot keep any liquids down at all, not even small sips of water or ice chips.
My mouth feels like sandpaper, and I have only urinated once today and it was a tiny amount of very dark tea-colored urine.
I am very thirsty because my mouth is parched, but I am not urinating frequently, and I have never had diabetes or used insulin.
No, I do not have any chest pain, chest tightness, or trouble breathing.
I have lost about four kilograms over the past two weeks since this nausea turned so severe.
I feel utterly exhausted and bedridden; even walking to the bathroom makes me feel like I might pass out.
No, I never induce vomiting or make myself throw up. It is completely involuntary.
I thought this was just a stubborn stomach bug layered on top of regular morning sickness.
I'm scared that being so dehydrated will hurt my baby, and I'm terrified my boss will fire me for missing more shifts.
I'm hoping to get IV fluids to stop the dizziness, medicine to stop the vomiting, and a doctor's note for my job.
I have always been healthy with no history of stomach ulcers, thyroid disease, or any chronic conditions.
I have never had any surgeries or previous hospital admissions.
I was prescribed prenatal vitamins two weeks ago, but they made me throw up immediately, so I stopped taking them three days ago.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I do not smoke cigarettes or vape, and I have never smoked.
I do not drink alcohol at all, especially now that I am pregnant.
I have never used marijuana, cannabis, or any recreational or illicit drugs.
I work as an office receptionist and live with my husband, but I have been on sick leave for the past three days because of this.
My mother told me she suffered from very bad nausea during her first trimester, but there is no family history of other major illnesses.
My last menstrual period started about eight weeks ago, and my cycles have always been regular every twenty-eight days.

exam.finding: Patient appears visibly exhausted and weak, lying still on the examination table with dry lips and sunken eyes.
Blood pressure is 96/62 mmHg, heart rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Blood pressure decreases to 84/52 mmHg and heart rate increases to 124 beats per minute upon standing, with notable lightheadedness.
Oral mucosa is dry with dry cracked lips and absent saliva pooling, while the posterior pharynx is clear without erythema.
Skin turgor is decreased with sluggish recoil, and capillary refill time is prolonged to three seconds.
Conjunctivae are pink, sclerae are non-icteric, pupils are equal and reactive to light, and no nystagmus is observed.
Neck is supple without cervical lymphadenopathy or jugular venous distension.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, non-tender, and without palpable nodules or bruits.
Heart sounds are tachycardic with regular rhythm, normal S1 and S2, and no audible murmurs or gallops.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with vesicular breath sounds and no wheezing or crackles.
Abdomen is scaphoid, non-distended, with no scars, visible peristalsis, or caput medusae.
Bowel sounds are present and normoactive in all four quadrants.
Abdomen is soft throughout with vague epigastric soreness from repeated dry heaving, but no focal tenderness or involuntary guarding.
No rebound tenderness or peritoneal signs are present.
Neck is completely supple with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
